title: Black Warrior Basin Mineral Rights
metaTitle: Sell Black Warrior Basin Mineral Rights | Alabama CBM
metaDescription: Own coalbed methane minerals or royalties in the Black Warrior Basin? Get a fair, no-obligation valuation grounded in Tuscaloosa Group production history.
heroLead: The Black Warrior Basin turned Alabama's coal country into the birthplace of commercial coalbed methane, and thousands of families still hold small mineral or royalty positions from that first wave of leasing.
intro: If your family's mineral interest traces back to Tuscaloosa, Jefferson, Walker, Fayette, or Pickens County, there is a decent chance it sits somewhere inside the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane fairway. This was the proving ground for CBM in the United States starting in the late 1970s, and the leasing that followed touched an enormous number of small landowners and heirs across west-central Alabama. Many of those original leases are decades old now, the wells that came with them are well into their production tail, and the royalty checks look nothing like they did in year one.

We work with owners across the basin who are trying to figure out what a mature CBM position is actually worth today, separate from what it might have been worth at the peak of drilling. That is a portfolio question as much as a geology question, and it is the one we spend the most time on with clients here.

sections.heading: Why the Black Warrior Basin Looks Different Than a Shale Play
paragraphs: Coalbed methane behaves on its own timeline compared with the horizontal shale wells most sellers hear about. Gas desorbs from coal seams in the Pottsville and Mary Lee coal groups as water is pumped off, so early production often ramps up before it declines, and the tail can run long and shallow rather than falling off a cliff in year two. That shape matters enormously when someone is putting a number on your interest, because a buyer discounting a Black Warrior royalty stream the same way they would discount a young shale well will usually undervalue it.

Most of the basin's wells were drilled a long time ago, which means the operators sitting on these leases today are frequently not the same companies that drilled them. Interests have changed hands through mergers, bankruptcies, and asset sales more than once. Before we ever discuss a number, we want to see who currently operates your unit and what the last several years of check stubs actually show, rather than only the lease terms from the original filing.

sections.heading: What Ownership Typically Looks Like Here
paragraphs: Because CBM leasing in the basin happened decades ago and touched so much rural, family-held acreage, undivided interests split across siblings and cousins are the norm rather than the exception. It is common for a single fractional mineral interest from a grandparent's original tract to have fractured into a dozen or more owners of record, each holding a sliver that individually pays very little but collectively still has real value if consolidated or benchmarked properly.

We also see a fair number of owners who inherited the interest with no lease history at all in hand, just old division order statements or a check that shows up (or stopped showing up) from an operator they do not recognize. Reconstructing that chain, from original patent or homestead through the current royalty deck, is routine work for us and something we do before we ever quote a number.

sections.heading: Valuing a Mature CBM Position
paragraphs: There is no honest single multiple we can quote you before we look at your specific decline curve, gas price exposure, and operator. Any range we give depends on how much production history you have, how flat or declining that curve looks over the trailing 12 to 36 months, whether the interest is producing or held-but-shut-in, and current natural gas pricing, which moves the value of a royalty stream more than almost anything else. We build our offer from your actual check history whenever you can provide it, rather than from a generic basin average.

Owners sometimes assume an old, small interest is not worth the paperwork to sell. In our experience it usually is, particularly for heirs who never intended to be in the oil and gas business and who would rather have a clean lump sum and one less tax form to track every year.

sections.heading: How We Handle the Paperwork
paragraphs: Alabama mineral title in the basin often runs through probate files, old severance deeds, and courthouse records in Tuscaloosa, Jefferson, Walker, Fayette, or Pickens County that were never fully digitized. We pull and review those records ourselves rather than asking you to chase them down, and we walk you through exactly what a closing package looks like before you sign anything. Depending on your circumstances there may be tax considerations worth discussing with your CPA before you sell, and we would rather flag that early than after closing.

faqs.question: Is my Black Warrior Basin interest even worth selling if the checks are small now?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. A small monthly check today can still represent a meaningful lump sum, especially when a buyer values the interest against remaining reserves and current gas pricing rather than just the most recent statement. We can tell you within a conversation or two whether it makes sense to pursue.

faqs.question: What if I only own a portion of the mineral interest, not the whole tract?
faqs.answer: Fractional and undivided interests are the norm in this basin, not the exception. We buy partial interests regularly and can work from whatever documentation you have, even if it is just a recent check stub or division order.

faqs.question: Does it matter which coal seam or operator is producing my interest?
faqs.answer: It does. Different operators report and pay differently, and different seams within the Pottsville and Mary Lee groups have different remaining life expectations. We look at operator and seam specifics as part of any valuation, beyond county location alone.

faqs.question: How long does a sale in the Black Warrior Basin typically take from offer to close?
faqs.answer: Once we have title records and recent production history in hand, most straightforward interests close within a few weeks. Interests with complicated heirship or unresolved probate can take longer, and we will tell you upfront if that applies to your situation.
